Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).

SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.

1	---
2	name: review-director-session-start
3	description: Review Director session 启动初始化流程——圆桌多轮审稿协议。Review Director 角色 session 启动时自动使用。
4	priority: 9
5	scope: global
6	tags:
7	- workflow
8	- review
9	- session
10	version: 3
11	roles:
12	- review_director
13	---
14	
15	# Review Director Session 启动流程（圆桌会议模式）
16	
17	## 初始化
18	
19	1. `director_get_project_overview(project)` — 了解研究现状（实验状态、最新报告）
20	2. 读取论文文件状态：检查 `projects/{project}/paper/` 或 `main.tex` 是否存在
21	3. 检查是否有来自 Research Director 的论文提交（`[论文提交]` 消息）
22	4. 向用户简要汇报：
23	   - **投稿目标**：venue 和 deadline
24	   - **论文状态**：当前草稿位置和版本
25	   - **资料完整性**：提交的材料是否齐全
26	   - **下一步**：即将开始的圆桌审稿流程
27	
28	## 评审流程（收到论文提交后执行）
29	
30	### Step 0 — 资料检查 + Venue 调研（必须先做，不可跳过）
31	
32	1. 检查提交资料完整性：论文文件是否存在、是否可读、补充材料是否齐全
33	2. 确认目标投稿 venue（从提交消息中获取）
34	3. 用 `web_search` 搜索该 venue 当前轮次的 CFP（Call for Papers），关键词示例：
35	   - `"<venue name> 2026 call for papers" site:aclweb.org`
36	   - `"<venue name> 2026 submission deadline"`
37	   - `"<venue name> 2026 author guidelines"`
38	4. **验证 deadline 未过期**：今天日期与截止日期对比，若已过期立即通知用户，不继续
39	5. 提取当前版本的格式要求：
40	   - 页数限制（正文 / 附录 / 参考文献）
41	   - 模板（ACL / IEEE / NeurIPS / ICML / ...）
42	   - 匿名规则（double-blind / single-blind / open）
43	   - 附录规则（是否允许、是否参与审稿）
44	   - 引用格式（natbib / biblatex / 特定 .bst）
45	6. 将以上信息作为上下文，随任务一起传递给 Reviewer
46	
47	⚠️ 禁止使用训练知识中的 venue 要求——格式标准每年都会更新，必须实时搜索确认。
48	
49	### Step 0.5 — 决定 Reviewer 编排
50	
51	根据 venue 类型和论文特点，决定：
52	- 需要几个 Reviewer（1-5 人）
53	- 每个 Reviewer 的审查侧重
54	
55	参考：
56	- **顶会长文**（NeurIPS/ICML/ACL）：3 人（方法/实验 + novelty/related work + 格式/ethics）
57	- **一般会议**（EMNLP/NAACL）：2 人（方法严谨性 + 新颖性/完整性）
58	- **Workshop / 短文**：1 人（全面审查）
59	
60	向 Group C（即项目配置中的 `feishu.review_chat_id` 审稿群）汇报编排决定。
61	
62	### Step 0.6 — 外部审稿线（与 Step 1 并行）
63	
64	检查项目配置中 `external_review.paperreview_ai.enabled` 是否为 `true`：
65	- 如果启用：调用 `request_external_review(project, paper_pdf_path, venue)` 向用户群发送协助提交卡片
66	- 这一步与 Step 1（内部 Reviewer 分配）**并行执行**，不阻塞内部审稿流程
67	- 外部结果到达后（用户在群里粘贴），纳入 Step 4 最终报告
68	- 如果到 Step 4 时外部结果仍未返回，调用 `get_external_review_status(project)` 确认状态，在报告中标注
69	
70	### Step 0.7 — 视觉审查派发（与 Step 1 并行）
71	
72	派发独立视觉审查 Agent，与 Reviewer 审稿并行执行：
73	
74	```
75	dispatch_visual_check(project="{project}", review_chat_id="{review_chat_id}")
76	```
77	
78	- 视觉审查 Agent 自动渲染论文 PDF 并逐页检查排版质量（Figure 1 位置、布局节奏、图表质量、空白分布等）
79	- **不参与评分和交叉讨论**，结果仅作为参考信息
80	- 启动和完成通知自动发送到 Group C
81	- 结果在 Step 4 通过 `get_visual_check_status(project)` 读取并拼入报告
82	- **fire-and-forget**：调用立即返回，本步骤永不等待视觉审查完成
83	
84	### Step 1 — Round N：独立审稿
85	
86	携带 Step 0 搜到的 venue 要求，启动所有 Reviewer：
87	
88	```
89	director_post_to_reviewer(reviewer_id="1", round_number=N, text="你负责 {focus}。...")
90	director_post_to_reviewer(reviewer_id="2", round_number=N, text="你负责 {focus}。...")
91	...（按需）
92	```
93	
94	消息中必须包含：
95	- venue 名称和截止日期
96	- 页数限制和模板名称
97	- 匿名规则
98	- 论文文件路径
99	- **该 Reviewer 的审查侧重**（在消息中明确指定）
100	
101	收集所有 Reviewer 的审稿结果。
102	
103	### Step 2 — 交叉分享（原文转发 + 逐条回应）
104	
105	将每位 Reviewer 的**完整审稿原文**转发给其他 Reviewer，要求逐条回应：
106	
107	```
108	director_post_to_reviewer(reviewer_id="2", round_number=N, text="""
109	以下是 Reviewer 1 的完整审稿意见：
110	
111	{Reviewer 1 的原文}
112	
113	请逐条回应：[AGREE] 同意并说明理由，或 [REBUT] 反驳并提供证据（cite 具体 Section/Table/Figure）。
114	""")
115	```
116	
117	对每位 Reviewer 重复此步骤（每人看到其他所有 Reviewer 的原文）。
118	
119	收集所有交叉回应。
120	
121	### Step 3 — 收敛判断
122	
123	分析所有 Reviewer 的意见和交叉回应：
124	
125	- **关键问题已达成共识**（`[AGREE]` 占多数，无未解决的 `[REBUT]` 矛盾）→ 进入 Step 4
126	- **存在重大分歧**（关键 issue 上有 `[REBUT]` 且双方各有道理）→ 回到 Step 1 开始下一轮，附带聚焦问题
127	- **最多 3 轮**：如果第 3 轮仍有分歧，在报告中如实记录各方观点
128	
129	### Step 4 — 汇总报告 & 投递
130	
131	合并所有轮次的发现，形成统一审稿报告：
132	
133	1. 报告结构：
134	   - **Summary**：论文概述（2-3 句）
135	   - **Strengths**：优点（逐条列出）
136	   - **Weaknesses**：缺点（逐条列出，这是重点，必须严格）
137	   - **Reviewer Consensus**：所有 Reviewer 达成共识的关键问题（标注 `[AGREE]`）
138	   - **Reviewer Divergence**：分歧点及各方理由（标注 `[REBUT]`，如有）
139	   - **Questions**：需要作者澄清的问题
140	   - **Missing References**：遗漏的重要相关工作
141	   - **External Review (Stanford Agentic Reviewer)**：如有外部审稿结果，单独列出其 7 维评分、关键发现、以及与内部审稿的差异；如未返回则标注状态
142	   - **Visual Layout Check**（非评分项，不阻塞报告）：调用 `get_visual_check_status(project)` 读一次状态——
143	     - `done` → 直接拼入 findings
144	     - `running` → 写"仍在进行中，本报告不等待，完成后会自动补发到 Group C"
145	     - `timeout` / `error` → 写失败原因 + 提示用户可重新触发
146	     - `not_started` → 写未派发
147	     不要为视觉审查推迟报告投递。视觉 Agent 完成后会自己把结果发到 Group C，与本报告解耦。可直接调用 `format_visual_findings_for_report(project)` 拿到现成的 markdown section
148	   - **Overall Assessment**：总评 + 评分（strong reject / weak reject / borderline / weak accept / strong accept）+ 置信度
149	   - **Detailed Comments**：逐节详细意见
150	2. **同步 Issue Tracker**（投递前必做）：
151	   - 用 `read_local_file("projects/{project}/artifacts/review_issues.yaml")` 读当前 tracker（不存在视为空）
152	   - 对本轮所有 Weakness/Must-Fix/Should-Fix:
153	     - 与已有 issue 匹配（同 category + 相似 summary）→ 在 `mentions` 追加本轮记录,更新 `last_seen_round`
154	     - 新问题 → 创建条目（id=`R{reviewer}-W{n}`,status=`open`,first_raised_round=本轮）
155	   - 对上轮 `open`/`in_progress` 但本轮**未被任何 Reviewer 提及**的:
156	     - 在 `mentions` 追加 `note: "本轮未提及,可能已修复,待 Research Director 确认"`
157	   - 调 `update_review_issues(project, issues_yaml=完整 YAML)` 写回
158	3. 调用 `submit_review_report_to_research_director` 投递报告 → Research Director
159	4. 向用户（Group C）汇报审核完成
160	
161	此流程只在 session 启动时执行一次。
162

# Review Director Session 启动流程（圆桌会议模式）

## 初始化

1. `director_get_project_overview(project)` — 了解研究现状（实验状态、最新报告）
2. 读取论文文件状态：检查 `projects/{project}/paper/` 或 `main.tex` 是否存在
3. 检查是否有来自 Research Director 的论文提交（`[论文提交]` 消息）
4. 向用户简要汇报：
   - **投稿目标**：venue 和 deadline
   - **论文状态**：当前草稿位置和版本
   - **资料完整性**：提交的材料是否齐全
   - **下一步**：即将开始的圆桌审稿流程

## 评审流程（收到论文提交后执行）

### Step 0 — 资料检查 + Venue 调研（必须先做，不可跳过）

1. 检查提交资料完整性：论文文件是否存在、是否可读、补充材料是否齐全
2. 确认目标投稿 venue（从提交消息中获取）
3. 用 `web_search` 搜索该 venue 当前轮次的 CFP（Call for Papers），关键词示例：
   - `"<venue name> 2026 call for papers" site:aclweb.org`
   - `"<venue name> 2026 submission deadline"`
   - `"<venue name> 2026 author guidelines"`
4. **验证 deadline 未过期**：今天日期与截止日期对比，若已过期立即通知用户，不继续
5. 提取当前版本的格式要求：
   - 页数限制（正文 / 附录 / 参考文献）
   - 模板（ACL / IEEE / NeurIPS / ICML / ...）
   - 匿名规则（double-blind / single-blind / open）
   - 附录规则（是否允许、是否参与审稿）
   - 引用格式（natbib / biblatex / 特定 .bst）
6. 将以上信息作为上下文，随任务一起传递给 Reviewer

⚠️ 禁止使用训练知识中的 venue 要求——格式标准每年都会更新，必须实时搜索确认。

### Step 0.5 — 决定 Reviewer 编排

根据 venue 类型和论文特点，决定：
- 需要几个 Reviewer（1-5 人）
- 每个 Reviewer 的审查侧重

参考：
- **顶会长文**（NeurIPS/ICML/ACL）：3 人（方法/实验 + novelty/related work + 格式/ethics）
- **一般会议**（EMNLP/NAACL）：2 人（方法严谨性 + 新颖性/完整性）
- **Workshop / 短文**：1 人（全面审查）

向 Group C（即项目配置中的 `feishu.review_chat_id` 审稿群）汇报编排决定。

### Step 0.6 — 外部审稿线（与 Step 1 并行）

检查项目配置中 `external_review.paperreview_ai.enabled` 是否为 `true`：
- 如果启用：调用 `request_external_review(project, paper_pdf_path, venue)` 向用户群发送协助提交卡片
- 这一步与 Step 1（内部 Reviewer 分配）**并行执行**，不阻塞内部审稿流程
- 外部结果到达后（用户在群里粘贴），纳入 Step 4 最终报告
- 如果到 Step 4 时外部结果仍未返回，调用 `get_external_review_status(project)` 确认状态，在报告中标注

### Step 0.7 — 视觉审查派发（与 Step 1 并行）

派发独立视觉审查 Agent，与 Reviewer 审稿并行执行：

```
dispatch_visual_check(project="{project}", review_chat_id="{review_chat_id}")
```

- 视觉审查 Agent 自动渲染论文 PDF 并逐页检查排版质量（Figure 1 位置、布局节奏、图表质量、空白分布等）
- **不参与评分和交叉讨论**，结果仅作为参考信息
- 启动和完成通知自动发送到 Group C
- 结果在 Step 4 通过 `get_visual_check_status(project)` 读取并拼入报告
- **fire-and-forget**：调用立即返回，本步骤永不等待视觉审查完成

### Step 1 — Round N：独立审稿

携带 Step 0 搜到的 venue 要求，启动所有 Reviewer：

```
director_post_to_reviewer(reviewer_id="1", round_number=N, text="你负责 {focus}。...")
director_post_to_reviewer(reviewer_id="2", round_number=N, text="你负责 {focus}。...")
...（按需）
```

消息中必须包含：
- venue 名称和截止日期
- 页数限制和模板名称
- 匿名规则
- 论文文件路径
- **该 Reviewer 的审查侧重**（在消息中明确指定）

收集所有 Reviewer 的审稿结果。

### Step 2 — 交叉分享（原文转发 + 逐条回应）

将每位 Reviewer 的**完整审稿原文**转发给其他 Reviewer，要求逐条回应：

```
director_post_to_reviewer(reviewer_id="2", round_number=N, text="""
以下是 Reviewer 1 的完整审稿意见：

{Reviewer 1 的原文}

请逐条回应：[AGREE] 同意并说明理由，或 [REBUT] 反驳并提供证据（cite 具体 Section/Table/Figure）。
""")
```

对每位 Reviewer 重复此步骤（每人看到其他所有 Reviewer 的原文）。

收集所有交叉回应。

### Step 3 — 收敛判断

分析所有 Reviewer 的意见和交叉回应：

- **关键问题已达成共识**（`[AGREE]` 占多数，无未解决的 `[REBUT]` 矛盾）→ 进入 Step 4
- **存在重大分歧**（关键 issue 上有 `[REBUT]` 且双方各有道理）→ 回到 Step 1 开始下一轮，附带聚焦问题
- **最多 3 轮**：如果第 3 轮仍有分歧，在报告中如实记录各方观点

### Step 4 — 汇总报告 & 投递

合并所有轮次的发现，形成统一审稿报告：

1. 报告结构：
   - **Summary**：论文概述（2-3 句）
   - **Strengths**：优点（逐条列出）
   - **Weaknesses**：缺点（逐条列出，这是重点，必须严格）
   - **Reviewer Consensus**：所有 Reviewer 达成共识的关键问题（标注 `[AGREE]`）
   - **Reviewer Divergence**：分歧点及各方理由（标注 `[REBUT]`，如有）
   - **Questions**：需要作者澄清的问题
   - **Missing References**：遗漏的重要相关工作
   - **External Review (Stanford Agentic Reviewer)**：如有外部审稿结果，单独列出其 7 维评分、关键发现、以及与内部审稿的差异；如未返回则标注状态
   - **Visual Layout Check**（非评分项，不阻塞报告）：调用 `get_visual_check_status(project)` 读一次状态——
     - `done` → 直接拼入 findings
     - `running` → 写"仍在进行中，本报告不等待，完成后会自动补发到 Group C"
     - `timeout` / `error` → 写失败原因 + 提示用户可重新触发
     - `not_started` → 写未派发
     不要为视觉审查推迟报告投递。视觉 Agent 完成后会自己把结果发到 Group C，与本报告解耦。可直接调用 `format_visual_findings_for_report(project)` 拿到现成的 markdown section
   - **Overall Assessment**：总评 + 评分（strong reject / weak reject / borderline / weak accept / strong accept）+ 置信度
   - **Detailed Comments**：逐节详细意见
2. **同步 Issue Tracker**（投递前必做）：
   - 用 `read_local_file("projects/{project}/artifacts/review_issues.yaml")` 读当前 tracker（不存在视为空）
   - 对本轮所有 Weakness/Must-Fix/Should-Fix:
     - 与已有 issue 匹配（同 category + 相似 summary）→ 在 `mentions` 追加本轮记录,更新 `last_seen_round`

## OOM 教训 (2026-05-20)
- 7.6GB RAM 机器上，N_SIM×n_items float64 矩阵不能一次性分配。MMLU 10K×14042×8B ≈ 1.07GB 单个矩阵，compute_lz_star 内部创建 ~7 个同尺寸中间数组 → OOM
- 解决方案：BATCH_SIZE=500 分批计算 + N_SIM 降至 2000（统计效力足够）
- generate_response 和 compute_lz_star 都需要分批

## Worker context exhaustion 教训 (2026-05-20)
- exp-v1-irt-refit-expanded Worker 跑 1.5 小时后崩溃，无输出。任务是从 HuggingFace 下载 500+ 模型的 per-item 数据并拟合 IRT。
- **根因**: 大量 HF API 调用 + 数据处理的累积输出耗尽 Worker context window。
- **教训**: 涉及大规模数据下载（100+ datasets）的任务必须分批 + checkpoint 中间结果，或拆成多个 Worker 串行执行。单个 Worker 不适合做 1.5hr+ 的重型数据工程。
- **补充 (同日)**: ssh_read_only 读取大 JSON 文件（8MB+ 单行）也会撑爆 context。Worker 操作远程大文件必须用 python 脚本提取摘要，不要 cat/head。
- **补充 (同日)**: Worker 无法在进程内长时间等待（~2 min 就退出）。涉及 GPU 训练 + eval 的任务应分阶段处理：训练完成后由 cron 回调触发 eval Worker，或由主 Agent 定时派 Worker 检查。

论文中标注为 "theoretical noise floor"，真实 SFT clean-vs-clean 在 ctrl-contam-pilot 中实现。

## exp-ml-classifier-baseline 关键发现 (2026-05-20)

**lz* 在低污染率 (5-10%) 优于有监督 ML 分类器**：5% contam lz* AUROC 0.675 vs best ML 0.575 (+0.10); 10% contam 0.763 vs 0.712 (+0.05)。ML 仅在 25%+ 污染时略胜 (+0.05)，但需 oracle contamination labels（实际不可用）。
RF feature importance 在 items 间高度弥散（top item <1%），与 lz* 全局 likelihood 方法一致。
论文限定为 simulation 场景下的对比，不推广为"所有 binary-only ML 方法都不如 IRT"。

## exp-domain-analysis 关键发现 (2026-05-20)

**Gemini-1.5 MMLU 100% accuracy 覆盖全部 57 个 subject**——不是 domain-concentrated 泄漏，是完全数据集泄漏。50/57 subjects flagged (lz*>1.96)，未 flagged 的 7 个 subject 的 lz* 也很高但 item 数太少。

**模型 contamination 指纹多样**：
- Doubao-pro: 反向 pattern，Humanities/Social Sciences lz* 极负（-13~-15），STEM 接近 0，Other 正向——可能是训练数据偏科
- Hunyuan-Turbo: STEM lz*=1.8 vs Social Sciences lz*=13.9——Social Sciences 方向过度拟合
- Yi-Lightning 和 Qwen-Plus: 全 domain 高 lz*（16~28），领先所有其他模型

**论文价值**: domain decomposition 为 12-model case study 增加定性分析深度，但 non-essential（P2 级别）。

**virology lz*=-8.21 诊断**：双重根因——(1) global θ=0.78 vs MMLU θ_MLE=4.0 错配；(2) virology 全部 166 items d<1.0 (mean=0.71)，即使 θ=4.0 仍有 58/166 items P<0.5。是 PSN-IRT calibration artifact，不影响 overall lz*=34.75。per-subject 分析需加 caveat。

## exp-natural-experiment 关键发现 (2026-05-20)

21 对 base→chat 模型 × 4 benchmarks（MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC-C/GSM8K）。

**两个 benchmark 有显著系统性 SFT 效应**：
- HellaSwag: Δlz* 偏差 mean=-3.40, t=-3.97, p=0.001（SFT 系统性降低 person-fit）
- GSM8K: Δlz* 偏差 mean=+3.92, t=3.35, p=0.009（SFT 系统性提高 person-fit）
- MMLU/ARC-C 无显著效应

**无个体 pair outlier**——未能检测到单个模型的 benchmark-specific contamination。
**Director 评估价值极低（P2-optional）**，不作为核心 evidence 使用。

## exp-4pl-ablation 关键发现 (2026-05-20)

**4PL d 参数对检测力的影响是决定性的，不是锦上添花。**

核心数据（4PL vs 3PL(d=1)，平均 power gain across contamination levels）：
- MMLU: +27.3pp (max +49.0pp)
- HellaSwag: +26.1pp (max +59.6pp)
- GSM8K: +20.3pp (max +39.7pp)
- ARC_C: +14.8pp (max +54.6pp)
- HumanEval: +13.7pp (max +30.6pp)

FAR 校准：4PL ≈ 5%（正确），3PL 4.7-16.5%（偏高），2PL 50-100%（完全不可用——固定 c=0.25 灾难性错误）。

**d-bucket 机制确认**：d<0.8 的 items 上 4PL 优势最大（MMLU +61pp），d≥0.95 时差异可忽略。这证实 d 参数捕捉 ceiling effect 是检测力提升的关键来源。

**论文价值**：回应 Reviewer R8 concern（为什么用 4PL 而非 3PL）。46% MMLU items d<0.95，忽略 d 约将检测力减半。这是 Method 部分的核心 justification。

## exp-4pl-real-data-degradation 关键发现 (2026-05-20)

**实数据验证：d 参数的影响对高能力模型是毁灭性的。**

在 12 个 PSN-IRT 模型的真实响应数据上，4PL vs 3PL(d=1) 的 lz* 仅有 r=0.225, RMSE=68.41——几乎无关联。

**不对称影响机制**：d=1 使 P(θ)→1（高能力模型预期全部答对），导致少量错误被 lz* 放大为极端异常值。低能力模型的 P(θ) 本身就远离 1.0，d=1 vs d<1 差异小，因此几乎不受影响。

- DeepSeek-V3 (θ=3.77): MMLU lz* 从 +16.4 暴跌至 -340.6
- Gemma-2B-it / Vicuna / Mistral (低 θ): |Δlz*|<2
- MMLU 最严重（46% items d<0.95），mean |Δlz*|=58.3

**与 exp-4pl-ablation 的互补**：ablation 在模拟数据上证明 power 损失，本实验在实数据上证明 lz* 值本身被完全摧毁。二者形成 R8 的双重证据链——4PL d 参数不可或缺。

**论文写作注意**：这个结果特别适合做 case study 可视化（选 DeepSeek-V3 on MMLU 作为 extreme case），放在 ablation study 或 appendix 中。

## exp-ctrl-contam-pilot 关键发现 (2026-05-20)

**首次真实 LLM controlled contamination 实验。** Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct QLoRA SFT，4+1 条件。

**核心结果（n=3 clean seeds, ddof=1）**：
| Condition | Accuracy | θ_MLE | lz* |
|-----------|----------|-------|-----|
| clean_s1 (seed=42) | 0.6787 | -0.0987 | 8.0101 |
| clean_s2 (seed=123) | 0.6789 | -0.0842 | 5.9440 |
| clean_s3 (seed=456) | 0.6783 | -0.1068 | 8.0806 |
| contam_15 | 0.7310 | +0.1971 | 3.0046 |
| contam_50 | 0.7644 | +0.3703 | 5.4480 |

**Baseline（n=3）**: mean=7.3449, std=1.2137
**Cohen's d（n=3, ddof=1）**: contam_15 d=-3.58, contam_50 d=-1.56
**注意**：之前汇报的 d=-3.85 / d=-1.48 使用了 ddof=0。论文统一用 ddof=1。

**H1 ✓ H2 ✓ H3 ✗(θ-free) H4 ✗**

**θ-shift 是 dose-response 倒置的确切原因**：
- contamination 抬高 θ_MLE（clean -0.09 → contam_50 +0.37），MLE 将 contamination 信号解释为 "能力提升"
- θ-fixed（固定为 clean θ 均值 -0.0914）下，dose-response 恢复单调：
  - |Δlz*_fixed_15| = 2.96, |Δlz*_fixed_50| = 8.67, ratio = 2.93 ✅
- θ-shift 分别吸收了 contam_15 的 6.93 和 contam_50 的 10.20 lz* 单位信号

**clean seed 变异性**：s1 和 s3 的 lz* 接近（8.01, 8.08），s2 明显低（5.94）。n=3 baseline std=1.21 vs n=2 的 1.46，加入 s3 压缩了方差，使 Cohen's d 更极端。

**Memorization fraction 低于预期**（0.38/0.29 vs 假设的 >0.5）——QLoRA 3 epochs 不足以产生强 memorization，但足以产生可检测的 lz* 偏移。

**论文叙事价值**：
1. θ-shift = "ability inflation" 是 contamination 逃避 person-fit 检测的核心机制
2. 与 simulation inverted-U 发现形成呼应——real-world 版本的同一现象
3. θ-fixed 分析作为 supplementary evidence 证明底层信号单调递增
4. 支撑 Discussion 中 "θ estimation as confound" 段落

## 跨模型族 controlled contamination 最终结论 (2026-05-21)

**三模型族 × 两污染水平 + ARC-C 跨 benchmark，n=10 clean seeds，bootstrap 95% CI**

| Model | Benchmark | d(15%) | 95% CI | d(50%) | 95% CI |
|-------|-----------|--------|--------|--------|--------|
| Qwen-2.5-7B | MMLU | -4.827 | [-14.29, -2.94] | -1.081 | [-3.93, -0.30] |
| Llama-3.1-8B | MMLU | -2.269 | [-4.63, -1.56] | -2.503 | [-5.19, -1.76] |
| Mistral-7B-v0.3 | MMLU | -2.636 | [-7.38, -1.49] | -3.496 | [-9.59, -2.09] |
| Qwen-2.5-7B | ARC-C | +3.161 | [+2.01, +9.54] | +5.303 | [+3.64, +15.49] |

**核心发现**：
- 所有 8 个 CI 排除零，跨模型族检测一致性确认
- Qwen 50% d 最弱 (-1.081)：θ-shift 吸收效应最强，与 pilot 阶段 θ-shift 分析一致
- Mistral clean 变异最大 (SD=2.052)：s2 (lz*=-1.05) 异常低，但 n=10 仍显著
- ARC-C 符号反转（正 d）：295 items 使 clean lz* 深度负值 (~-5.4)，污染使其"更不负"
- **dose-response 非单调**：Qwen/Llama |d(15%)| > |d(50%)|，Mistral 相反——inverted-U + θ-shift 交互效应

**决策依据**：n=10 提供足够统计效力，bootstrap CI 不依赖正态假设。Qwen 的 n=10 值从 individual seed lz*（post-Snijders correction）重算，替代早期 n=3 结果。

Review versions of long papers may have up to eight (8) pages of content plus unlimited pages for references, while review versions of short papers may have up to four (4) pages of content, plus unlimited pages for references. \section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Benchmark contamination, the unintended inclusion of evaluation data in training corpora, poses a growing threat to the integrity of large language model (LLM) evaluation \citep{dodge2021, magar2022, sainz2023}.
As training corpora and public benchmarks both expand, the probability of overlap increases structurally \citep{jacovi2023, chang2024survey}.
When contamination occurs, benchmark scores no longer reflect genuine capability, undermining the primary mechanism by which the community compares and selects models.

A range of detection methods have been proposed, but all require some form of privileged access beyond the binary response record.
N-gram overlap methods need the training corpus \citep{dodge2021, magar2022}.
Membership inference approaches require token-level probabilities \citep{minkprob2024, deng2024}.
Probing methods rely on crafted prompts \citep{golchin2024, oren2024}.
Performance-based methods require multiple test variants or output logits \citep{constat2024, codec2026}.
These methods form a detection frontier ordered by information access.
No existing method operates at the bottom of this frontier: binary response patterns alone.

The need for minimal-information detection grows more pressing as models evolve.
\citet{wang2025fragility} show that all ten log-probability-based methods they evaluate perform at chance level on models trained with reinforcement learning (RL), because RL reshapes internal token distributions while preserving binary correctness patterns.
This motivates a fundamental question: \emph{what can binary response patterns reveal about contamination, and under what conditions?}

We observe that a contaminated LLM is functionally analogous to a test-taker with item preknowledge: both produce response patterns in which difficult items are answered correctly through memorization rather than genuine ability.
This connection points to person-fit statistics, developed over four decades for cheating detection in educational testing \citep{drasgow1985, meijer2001, karabatsos2003, sinharay2017}.
The standardized statistic $\ell_z^*$ \citep{snijders2001} measures how well a response pattern conforms to Item Response Theory (IRT) model predictions.
Figure~\ref{fig:motivation} illustrates this analogy.
Despite the natural correspondence, no prior work has applied person-fit statistics to LLM benchmark contamination.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig_1_response_pattern.pdf}
  \caption{A clean model's responses track the IRT-predicted probability curve (left); a contaminated model shows anomalous successes on hard items (right, red diamonds), producing a large $|\Delta\ell_z^*|$ signal.}
  \label{fig:motivation}
\end{figure}

Rather than proposing $\ell_z^*$ as a ready-to-deploy detection tool, we systematically characterize the behavior boundaries of IRT person-fit statistics for LLM contamination detection.
Using controlled contamination experiments across three model families (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B; $n{=}10$ seeds each) with pre-calibrated 4PL item parameters from PSN-IRT \citep{psnirt2026}, we identify four IRT-specific findings on MMLU \citep{hendrycks2021mmlu} and ARC-Challenge:

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
\item \textbf{Non-monotonic dose-response.} Under free-$\theta$ estimation, detection strength ($|d|$) is non-monotonic between 15\% and 50\% contamination: Qwen shows $|d|{=}6.58$ at 15\% but only $|d|{=}1.90$ at 50\%, because $\theta$-shift absorption attenuates the signal at higher contamination. Fixed-$\theta$ estimation restores monotonicity for models with stable clean baselines, substantially amplifying detection at high contamination levels for high-ability models.

\item \textbf{Model-specific $\theta$-shift dynamics.} Baseline model ability modulates detection sensitivity: lower-ability models (Mistral, 52.4\% accuracy) show stronger signals ($|d|{=}3.50$) than higher-ability models (Qwen, 67.8\%, $|d|{=}1.90$) at 50\% contamination. ARC-C (295 items) reverses this pattern through a ceiling effect.

\item \textbf{Detection-diagnosis tradeoff.} Simpler statistics yield stronger detection: accuracy $z$-scores produce $|d|$ values several-fold to over an order of magnitude larger than person-fit statistics, and HT generally exceeds $\ell_z^*$. Yet the diagnostic power reverses: only $\ell_z^*$ supports seen/unseen decomposition, mechanistic $\theta$-shift analysis, and sensitivity to response-pattern structure (57/60 vs.\ 4/60 flagged cells on real-world data).

\item \textbf{Post-RL residual pattern (preliminary).} In a single-model pilot ($N{=}1$, Qwen, GRPO), GRPO training erases the accuracy gap between seen and unseen items ($11.4\text{pp} \to 2.1\text{pp}$), but the $\ell_z^*$ response-pattern gap persists (${\sim}3.3$). No statistical inference is drawn from this observation.
\end{enumerate}

Our contributions are threefold:
(1) We provide the first systematic characterization of IRT person-fit behavior for LLM contamination, identifying boundary conditions ($\theta$-shift, benchmark size, model ability) that determine when and why detection succeeds or fails.
(2) We establish that $\Delta\ell_z^*$ reliably detects SFT-stage contamination across three model families (all bootstrap 95\% CIs exclude zero, $n{=}10$).
(3) We document the detection-diagnosis tradeoff and post-RL boundary, clarifying what binary response patterns can and cannot reveal.

1	\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related_work}
2	
3	\paragraph{Benchmark contamination detection.}
4	Contamination detection methods span a wide range of information requirements.
5	Corpus-search methods match benchmark items directly against pretraining data \citep{dodge2021, magar2022}, but require full corpus access unavailable for closed models.
6	Membership inference attacks (MIA) use token-level log-probabilities to distinguish training from unseen examples \citep{minkprob2024, deng2024}.
7	Generation-based probes elicit benchmark content via prompting \citep{golchin2024, golchin2024quiz, oren2024}.
8	Performance-based methods compare accuracy on target and reference sets \citep{constat2024, codec2026}, requiring multiple evaluations or in-context learning passes.
9	\citet{sainz2023} argue for systematic per-benchmark contamination measurement, and \citet{jacovi2023} propose mitigation strategies including encrypted benchmarks and canary strings.
10	
11	A critical limitation unites all token-level methods: \citet{wang2025fragility} show that RL post-training renders MIA-based detectors no better than random across 10 methods and 4 benchmarks, because RL reshapes token distributions while largely preserving binary correctness patterns.
12	\citet{selfcritique2026} and \citet{zhang2026rlvr} propose RL-specific solutions but require generation-level access.
13	Our approach operates at the minimal information point: binary responses only.
14	
15	\paragraph{IRT for LLM evaluation.}
16	Item Response Theory has seen growing adoption in NLP and ML evaluation.
17	\citet{martinezplumed2019} applied IRT to analyze machine learning classifiers at the instance level, establishing that item difficulty and discrimination parameters capture meaningful variation across models.
18	\citet{lalor2019} proposed estimating IRT parameters from DNN-generated response patterns, removing the need for human annotators.
19	\citet{rodriguez2021} demonstrated that IRT-informed item weighting improves leaderboard rankings over raw accuracy.
20	\citet{polo2024tinybenchmarks} used IRT-based item selection to reduce benchmark sizes by 100$\times$ while preserving model rankings, and \citet{atlas2025} developed adaptive testing procedures for efficient LLM evaluation.
21	Most directly relevant, \citet{psnirt2026} calibrated 4PL item parameters for over 13,000 models across 11 benchmarks, providing the item bank our framework builds on.
22	All of these works use IRT for ability estimation or benchmark efficiency; none apply \emph{person-fit} statistics for contamination detection.
23	
24	\paragraph{Person-fit statistics in psychometrics.}
25	Person-fit analysis has a long history in educational measurement for detecting aberrant test-taking behavior, including cheating and item preknowledge.
26	\citet{drasgow1985} introduced $\ell_z$, a standardized log-likelihood residual; \citet{snijders2001} derived the corrected $\ell_z^*$ that accounts for ability estimation uncertainty.
27	\citet{karabatsos2003} compared 36 person-fit statistics and found $\ell_z$ among the most powerful for detecting cheating.
28	\citet{vanderflier1982} introduced the U3 statistic for nonparametric detection of deviant response patterns, and \citet{meijer2001} provide a comprehensive review of person-fit methodology.
29	\citet{sinharay2017} showed that $\ell_z^*$ is particularly effective when the set of compromised items is known, a setting analogous to benchmark contamination where memorized items constitute the compromised set.
30	Our work transfers this psychometric toolkit to LLM evaluation, treating each model as an examinee whose item-level response pattern may reveal memorization.

\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related_work}

\paragraph{Benchmark contamination detection.}
Contamination detection methods span a wide range of information requirements.
Corpus-search methods match benchmark items directly against pretraining data \citep{dodge2021, magar2022}, but require full corpus access unavailable for closed models.
Membership inference attacks (MIA) use token-level log-probabilities to distinguish training from unseen examples \citep{minkprob2024, deng2024}.
Generation-based probes elicit benchmark content via prompting \citep{golchin2024, golchin2024quiz, oren2024}.
Performance-based methods compare accuracy on target and reference sets \citep{constat2024, codec2026}, requiring multiple evaluations or in-context learning passes.
\citet{sainz2023} argue for systematic per-benchmark contamination measurement, and \citet{jacovi2023} propose mitigation strategies including encrypted benchmarks and canary strings.

A critical limitation unites all token-level methods: \citet{wang2025fragility} show that RL post-training renders MIA-based detectors no better than random across 10 methods and 4 benchmarks, because RL reshapes token distributions while largely preserving binary correctness patterns.
\citet{selfcritique2026} and \citet{zhang2026rlvr} propose RL-specific solutions but require generation-level access.
Our approach operates at the minimal information point: binary responses only.

\paragraph{IRT for LLM evaluation.}
Item Response Theory has seen growing adoption in NLP and ML evaluation.
\citet{martinezplumed2019} applied IRT to analyze machine learning classifiers at the instance level, establishing that item difficulty and discrimination parameters capture meaningful variation across models.
\citet{lalor2019} proposed estimating IRT parameters from DNN-generated response patterns, removing the need for human annotators.
\citet{rodriguez2021} demonstrated that IRT-informed item weighting improves leaderboard rankings over raw accuracy.
\citet{polo2024tinybenchmarks} used IRT-based item selection to reduce benchmark sizes by 100$\times$ while preserving model rankings, and \citet{atlas2025} developed adaptive testing procedures for efficient LLM evaluation.
Most directly relevant, \citet{psnirt2026} calibrated 4PL item parameters for over 13,000 models across 11 benchmarks, providing the item bank our framework builds on.
All of these works use IRT for ability estimation or benchmark efficiency; none apply \emph{person-fit} statistics for contamination detection.

\paragraph{Person-fit statistics in psychometrics.}
Person-fit analysis has a long history in educational measurement for detecting aberrant test-taking behavior, including cheating and item preknowledge.
\citet{drasgow1985} introduced $\ell_z$, a standardized log-likelihood residual; \citet{snijders2001} derived the corrected $\ell_z^*$ that accounts for ability estimation uncertainty.
\citet{karabatsos2003} compared 36 person-fit statistics and found $\ell_z$ among the most powerful for detecting cheating.
\citet{vanderflier1982} introduced the U3 statistic for nonparametric detection of deviant response patterns, and \citet{meijer2001} provide a comprehensive review of person-fit methodology.
\citet{sinharay2017} showed that $\ell_z^*$ is particularly effective when the set of compromised items is known, a setting analogous to benchmark contamination where memorized items constitute the compromised set.
Our work transfers this psychometric toolkit to LLM evaluation, treating each model as an examinee whose item-level response pattern may reveal memorization.

1	\section{Results}
2	\label{sec:results}
3	
4	\subsection{Detection Signal Across Model Families}
5	\label{sec:detection}
6	
7	Table~\ref{tab:cohens_d} presents Cohen's $d$ effect sizes for $\ell_z^*$ across three model families and two benchmarks.
8	All confidence intervals exclude zero, confirming that $\Delta\ell_z^*$ reliably separates contaminated from clean models at both contamination levels.
9	
10	On MMLU, effect sizes range from $|d|{=}1.90$ (Qwen at 50\%) to $|d|{=}6.58$ (Qwen at 15\%), with Llama ($|d|{=}2.27$/$2.50$) and Mistral ($|d|{=}2.64$/$3.50$) falling between.
11	On ARC-C (295 items), Qwen yields $|d|{=}3.16$ at 15\% and $|d|{=}5.30$ at 50\%, demonstrating that detection remains feasible even on small benchmarks when contamination is sufficiently concentrated.
12	
13	Clean-model $\ell_z^*$ baselines diverge substantially across families: Qwen ${+}8.68$ ($\text{SD}{=}0.74$), Mistral ${+}4.02$ ($\text{SD}{=}2.05$), Llama ${+}0.29$ ($\text{SD}{=}1.45$), and ARC-C Qwen ${-}5.42$ ($\text{SD}{=}0.16$).
14	Absolute $\ell_z^*$ thresholds would produce contradictory results: Qwen's contaminated $\ell_z^*$ at 15\% (${+}3.85$) is still positive.
15	The $\Delta\ell_z^*$ design normalizes these divergent baselines: Cohen's $d$ yields comparable effect sizes ($|d|{=}1.90$--$6.58$) despite order-of-magnitude baseline differences.
16	Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap} provides a visual summary.
17	
18	\begin{table}[t]
19	\centering
20	\caption{Cohen's $d$ for $\Delta\ell_z^*$ across model families ($n{=}10$ clean seeds, bootstrap 95\% CI, 10,000 resamples). All CIs exclude 0.}
21	\label{tab:cohens_d}
22	\footnotesize
23	\begin{tabular}{@{}llrr@{}}
24	\toprule
25	Model & Benchmark & $d$ (15\%) [CI] & $d$ (50\%) [CI] \\
26	\midrule
27	Qwen & MMLU & $-6.58$ [$-15.2$, $-4.5$] & $-1.90$ [$-5.0$, $-1.0$] \\
28	Llama & MMLU & $-2.27$ [$-4.6$, $-1.6$] & $-2.50$ [$-5.0$, $-1.8$] \\
29	Mistral & MMLU & $-2.64$ [$-7.4$, $-1.5$] & $-3.50$ [$-9.6$, $-2.1$] \\
30	Qwen & ARC-C & $+3.16$ [$2.0$, $9.5$] & $+5.30$ [$3.6$, $15.2$] \\
31	\bottomrule
32	\end{tabular}
33	\end{table}
34	
35	\begin{figure*}[t]
36	  \centering
37	  \includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_heatmap.pdf}
38	  \caption{Cohen's $|d|$ heatmap for contamination detection across three model families and two benchmarks. Blue intensity reflects effect-size magnitude. Values and 95\% bootstrap CIs annotated per cell. Grey cells indicate missing conditions (Llama and Mistral on ARC-C not included in the current study).}
39	  \label{fig:heatmap}
40	\end{figure*}
41	
42	\subsection{Non-Monotonic Dose-Response}
43	\label{sec:inverted_u}
44	
45	Under free-$\theta$ estimation, the dose-response relationship between contamination level and $|\Delta\ell_z^*|$ is non-monotonic for high-baseline-misfit models.
46	Qwen exhibits a striking inversion: $|d|{=}6.58$ at 15\% contamination but only $|d|{=}1.90$ at 50\%, a 3.5$\times$ reduction in detection strength at higher contamination.
47	This non-monotonic pattern (observed between two non-zero contamination levels; intermediate points were not sampled) is an IRT-specific phenomenon absent from accuracy-based statistics.
48	
49	The mechanism is $\theta$-shift absorption.
50	Contamination raises overall accuracy, which inflates $\hat{\theta}_{\text{MLE}}$.
51	A higher $\hat{\theta}$ ``explains away'' the anomalous successes on hard items, absorbing the contamination signal into the ability estimate.
52	At 50\% contamination, $\hat{\theta}$ shifts further ($\Delta\theta{=}0.47$) than at 15\% ($\Delta\theta{=}0.29$ for Qwen), so the residual $\ell_z^*$ signal shrinks despite greater actual contamination.
53	
54	The non-monotonic pattern is model-dependent.
55	Mistral, with lower baseline accuracy (52.4\%) and lower baseline misfit ($\ell_z^*{=}{+}4.02$), exhibits monotonic free-$\theta$ dose-response: $|d|$ increases from 2.64 to 3.50 as contamination rises from 15\% to 50\%.
56	Llama (baseline accuracy 59.3\%) is nearly monotonic, with $|d|$ increasing from 2.27 to 2.50.
57	The critical variable is baseline ability: higher-ability models have less $\theta$-shift headroom, leaving more of the contamination signal as an IRT residual at lower contamination levels, but then absorbing it as the contamination fraction grows.
58	
59	Fixed-$\theta$ estimation resolves the inversion for models with stable clean baselines (Qwen, Mistral), but not for models with high cross-seed $\ell_z^*$ variance (Llama), where free-$\theta$ estimation already provides adequate detection.
60	Anchoring $\theta$ at the clean-model mean eliminates the absorption mechanism, producing monotonic dose-response: for Qwen and Mistral, fixed-$\theta$ $|d|$ substantially exceeds free-$\theta$ $|d|$ at 50\% contamination (Table~\ref{tab:theta_fixed}).
61	The apparent weak free-$\theta$ detection at high contamination is an artifact of $\theta$ re-estimation, not signal absence.
62	In practice, fixed-$\theta$ requires either a pre-contamination reference or cross-benchmark ability estimation.
63	
64	A simulated power analysis corroborates these findings: two-sided testing (flagging both large negative and large positive $\ell_z^*$) achieves ${>}$93\% power on MMLU at all contamination levels, with the theoretical power function yielding $R^2 {=} 0.957$ against simulated values (Appendix~\ref{app:simulation}).
65	
66	\subsection{Model-Specific $\theta$-Shift Dynamics}
67	\label{sec:theta_dynamics}
68	
69	The $\theta$-shift mechanism interacts with baseline model ability to produce an observed trend: higher-ability models show weaker detection signals under free-$\theta$ estimation at high contamination.
70	Figure~\ref{fig:theta_scatter} plots baseline accuracy against Cohen's $|d|$ for all model-benchmark combinations.
71	
72	On MMLU, a negative correlation emerges between baseline accuracy and $|d|$ at 50\% contamination: Mistral (52.4\% accuracy, $|d|{=}3.50$) $>$ Llama (59.3\%, $|d|{=}2.50$) $>$ Qwen (67.8\%, $|d|{=}1.90$).
73	The explanation is geometric: a model already near the asymptotic ceiling of most item characteristic curves gains less $\hat{\theta}$ from contamination-induced accuracy boosts, but the reduced $\theta$-shift headroom leaves less room for the ability estimate to absorb the aberrance signal.
74	At 15\% contamination, the pattern is less pronounced because the $\theta$-shift is smaller in absolute terms, leaving a larger proportion of the signal as residual aberrance.
75	
76	ARC-C reverses this pattern.
77	Despite Qwen's high baseline accuracy on ARC-C (90.0\%), contamination produces larger, not smaller, effect sizes ($|d|{=}3.16$ at 15\%, $|d|{=}5.30$ at 50\%).
78	This reversal reflects a ceiling effect: with only 295 items and 90.0\% baseline accuracy, the already-correct items offer minimal room for further $\theta$ inflation, so contamination manifests primarily as anomalous successes on the few remaining hard items.
79	The small item count amplifies this concentration, producing a disproportionately large $\ell_z^*$ shift per contaminated item.
80	
81	The baseline $\ell_z^*$ for ARC-C is negative ($-5.42$), in contrast to the positive baselines on MMLU.
82	This sign difference reflects the interaction between benchmark item parameters and model ability: on ARC-C, the 4PL model expects near-perfect performance from a high-ability model, so the clean response pattern appears over-consistent rather than aberrant.
83	Contamination pushes $\ell_z^*$ further positive (toward zero), producing the positive Cohen's $d$ values in Table~\ref{tab:cohens_d}.
84	
85	These findings indicate that detection sensitivity is not a fixed property of $\ell_z^*$ but depends on the interaction between model ability and benchmark characteristics, a consideration absent from standard person-fit applications.
86	
87	\paragraph{Fixed-$\theta$ estimation.}
88	Table~\ref{tab:theta_fixed} compares free-$\theta$ and fixed-$\theta$ Cohen's $d$ across all three families.
89	The benefit of fixed-$\theta$ is strongly modulated by baseline ability.
90	Qwen (67.8\% accuracy) shows the largest amplification, because the high baseline provides substantial $\theta$-shift headroom that free estimation exploits to absorb the signal.
91	Mistral (52.4\%) shows moderate amplification (1.6$\times$ at 50\%), consistent with intermediate baseline ability.
92	Llama (59.3\%) shows no benefit from fixed-$\theta$: its high cross-seed $\ell_z^*$ variance ($\text{SD}{=}1.45$ vs.\ Qwen's $0.16$ on ARC-C) inflates the denominator, and its free-$\theta$ estimates are already monotonic ($|d|{=}2.27 \to 2.50$).
93	The Llama result is itself informative: fixed-$\theta$ estimation is indicated for models with stable clean baselines and high $\theta$-shift absorption (Qwen, Mistral), not as a universal remedy.

125	\subsection{Detection-Diagnosis Tradeoff}
126	\label{sec:degradation}
127	
128	A natural question is whether the full 4PL IRT framework is necessary for contamination detection, or whether simpler statistics suffice.
129	Table~\ref{tab:degradation} compares three statistics at decreasing levels of information access: $\ell_z^*$ (requires 4PL parameters $a, b, c, d$), the HT statistic (requires only difficulty $b$), and an accuracy $z$-score (requires no item parameters).
130	
131	The comparison reveals a detection-diagnosis tradeoff.
132	For pure detection, simpler statistics are more powerful: accuracy $z$-scores yield $|d|$ values several-fold to over an order of magnitude larger than person-fit statistics ($|d|{=}68.7$ vs.\ $|d|{=}1.90$ for Qwen at 50\%), because cross-seed accuracy variance is near-zero in controlled settings.
133	HT generally exceeds $\ell_z^*$ in detection strength (e.g., Qwen 15\%: $|d_{\text{HT}}|{=}7.26$ vs.\ $|d_{\ell_z^*}|{=}6.58$), since HT is not attenuated by the Snijders correction for $\theta$ estimation uncertainty.
134	Both person-fit statistics exhibit the non-monotonic pattern (Qwen HT: $|d|{=}7.26$ at 15\% vs.\ $|d|{=}1.66$ at 50\%), confirming that $\theta$-shift absorption is a general property of statistics conditioned on ability, not an artifact of $\ell_z^*$ specifically.
135	
136	Yet the diagnostic power reverses.
137	Full IRT parameterization is unnecessary for mere detection, but the value of $\ell_z^*$ lies in three capabilities that HT and $z$-scores lack:
138	(a) \emph{seen/unseen decomposition}: $\ell_z^*$ can be computed separately on seen and unseen item subsets, though item-level detection is near-random (AUROC $\approx 0.53$; Appendix~\ref{app:item_auroc}), confirming that the contamination signal is diffuse and requires model-level aggregation;
139	(b) \emph{$\theta$-shift mechanism}: the ability parameter exposes why detection sensitivity depends on model ability (\S\ref{sec:theta_dynamics}), a mechanistic insight inaccessible to non-parametric statistics;
140	(c) \emph{structural sensitivity}: on real leaderboard data, $\ell_z^*$ flags 57/60 model-benchmark cells as aberrant---evidence of systematic IRT assumption violations that motivates the $\Delta\ell_z^*$ differencing design (\S\ref{sec:did}).
141	Accuracy $z$-scores flag only 4/60 cells, making them insensitive to the response-pattern structure that $\ell_z^*$ exploits for within-model diagnosis.
142	While such patterns have theoretical antecedents in person-fit literature \citep{stonge2011}, the specific magnitude and model-dependence we observe are new empirical findings in the LLM domain; nonparametric alternatives \citep{tendeiro2014} may complement $\ell_z^*$ where 4PL calibration is unavailable.
143	
144	In practice, a two-stage workflow follows from this tradeoff: a practitioner would first screen for contamination using accuracy $z$-scores (which yield $|d|{=}68.7$ for Qwen at 50\%), then apply $\ell_z^*$ to characterize the mechanism---whether the signal reflects $\theta$-shift absorption (indicating high-baseline models requiring fixed-$\theta$ anchoring) or uniform aberrance (suggesting direct item memorization).
145	
146	Within the IRT family, the 4PL specification matters: simulation ablations show a mean $+$27.3pp power gain over 3PL on MMLU, because 46\% of MMLU items have upper asymptote $d < 0.95$, and the 3PL model (which assumes $d{=}1$) misattributes slip-related response patterns as aberrance (Appendix~\ref{app:4pl_ablation}).

173	\subsection{Preliminary Observation: Post-RL Residual Pattern}
174	\label{sec:post_rl}
175	
176	Deployed LLMs undergo reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) or related post-training \citep{ouyang2022, rafailov2023}, which may obscure contamination signals established during SFT.
177	\citet{wang2025fragility} show that all existing MIA-based detectors fail after post-RL training.
178	We apply GRPO to a Qwen model contaminated at 15\% on MMLU and track both accuracy and $\ell_z^*$ across training steps.
179	
180	Figure~\ref{fig:grpo} reveals a dual finding.
181	First, GRPO erases the accuracy gap between seen and unseen items: the SFT baseline shows 83.1\% accuracy on seen items versus 71.7\% on unseen (a gap of 11.4pp), but after 1,500 GRPO steps, the gap shrinks to 2.1pp (73.2\% vs.\ 71.1\%).
182	Accuracy-based contamination detection faces a hard boundary at this point.
183	
184	Second, the $\ell_z^*$ response-pattern structure persists despite the accuracy equalization.
185	SFT produces $\ell_z^*{=}2.91$; after 1,500 GRPO steps, $\ell_z^*{=}7.69$ (an increase, not a decrease, reflecting model reorganization toward higher overall ability).
186	The seen-unseen $\ell_z^*$ gap remains at approximately 3.3 ($\ell_{z,\text{seen}}^{*}{=}3.54$ vs.\ $\ell_{z,\text{unseen}}^{*}{=}6.86$), indicating that item-level response patterns retain structural traces of the contamination even after the aggregate accuracy difference disappears.
187	The $\ell_z^*$ trajectory stabilizes after step 500: all metrics change by less than 3\% between subsequent checkpoints, suggesting a plateau.
188	
189	This result is $N{=}1$ (Qwen only, 15\% MMLU, GRPO) and carries important caveats: the persistence of the $\ell_z^*$ gap does not constitute proof that contamination is detectable post-RL in deployment, since the gap magnitude and sign may vary with different model families, contamination levels, and RL methods (PPO, DPO).
190	We report this as a preliminary characterization of the post-RL boundary condition.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

\subsection{Detection Signal Across Model Families}
\label{sec:detection}

Table~\ref{tab:cohens_d} presents Cohen's $d$ effect sizes for $\ell_z^*$ across three model families and two benchmarks.
All confidence intervals exclude zero, confirming that $\Delta\ell_z^*$ reliably separates contaminated from clean models at both contamination levels.

On MMLU, effect sizes range from $|d|{=}1.90$ (Qwen at 50\%) to $|d|{=}6.58$ (Qwen at 15\%), with Llama ($|d|{=}2.27$/$2.50$) and Mistral ($|d|{=}2.64$/$3.50$) falling between.
On ARC-C (295 items), Qwen yields $|d|{=}3.16$ at 15\% and $|d|{=}5.30$ at 50\%, demonstrating that detection remains feasible even on small benchmarks when contamination is sufficiently concentrated.

Clean-model $\ell_z^*$ baselines diverge substantially across families: Qwen ${+}8.68$ ($\text{SD}{=}0.74$), Mistral ${+}4.02$ ($\text{SD}{=}2.05$), Llama ${+}0.29$ ($\text{SD}{=}1.45$), and ARC-C Qwen ${-}5.42$ ($\text{SD}{=}0.16$).
Absolute $\ell_z^*$ thresholds would produce contradictory results: Qwen's contaminated $\ell_z^*$ at 15\% (${+}3.85$) is still positive.
The $\Delta\ell_z^*$ design normalizes these divergent baselines: Cohen's $d$ yields comparable effect sizes ($|d|{=}1.90$--$6.58$) despite order-of-magnitude baseline differences.
Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap} provides a visual summary.

\subsection{Non-Monotonic Dose-Response}
\label{sec:inverted_u}

Under free-$\theta$ estimation, the dose-response relationship between contamination level and $|\Delta\ell_z^*|$ is non-monotonic for high-baseline-misfit models.
Qwen exhibits a striking inversion: $|d|{=}6.58$ at 15\% contamination but only $|d|{=}1.90$ at 50\%, a 3.5$\times$ reduction in detection strength at higher contamination.
This non-monotonic pattern (observed between two non-zero contamination levels; intermediate points were not sampled) is an IRT-specific phenomenon absent from accuracy-based statistics.

The mechanism is $\theta$-shift absorption.
Contamination raises overall accuracy, which inflates $\hat{\theta}_{\text{MLE}}$.
A higher $\hat{\theta}$ ``explains away'' the anomalous successes on hard items, absorbing the contamination signal into the ability estimate.
At 50\% contamination, $\hat{\theta}$ shifts further ($\Delta\theta{=}0.47$) than at 15\% ($\Delta\theta{=}0.29$ for Qwen), so the residual $\ell_z^*$ signal shrinks despite greater actual contamination.

The non-monotonic pattern is model-dependent.
Mistral, with lower baseline accuracy (52.4\%) and lower baseline misfit ($\ell_z^*{=}{+}4.02$), exhibits monotonic free-$\theta$ dose-response: $|d|$ increases from 2.64 to 3.50 as contamination rises from 15\% to 50\%.
Llama (baseline accuracy 59.3\%) is nearly monotonic, with $|d|$ increasing from 2.27 to 2.50.
The critical variable is baseline ability: higher-ability models have less $\theta$-shift headroom, leaving more of the contamination signal as an IRT residual at lower contamination levels, but then absorbing it as the contamination fraction grows.

Fixed-$\theta$ estimation resolves the inversion for models with stable clean baselines (Qwen, Mistral), but not for models with high cross-seed $\ell_z^*$ variance (Llama), where free-$\theta$ estimation already provides adequate detection.
Anchoring $\theta$ at the clean-model mean eliminates the absorption mechanism, producing monotonic dose-response: for Qwen and Mistral, fixed-$\theta$ $|d|$ substantially exceeds free-$\theta$ $|d|$ at 50\% contamination (Table~\ref{tab:theta_fixed}).
The apparent weak free-$\theta$ detection at high contamination is an artifact of $\theta$ re-estimation, not signal absence.
In practice, fixed-$\theta$ requires either a pre-contamination reference or cross-benchmark ability estimation.

A simulated power analysis corroborates these findings: two-sided testing (flagging both large negative and large positive $\ell_z^*$) achieves ${>}$93\% power on MMLU at all contamination levels, with the theoretical power function yielding $R^2 {=} 0.957$ against simulated values (Appendix~\ref{app:simulation}).

\subsection{Model-Specific $\theta$-Shift Dynamics}
\label{sec:theta_dynamics}

The $\theta$-shift mechanism interacts with baseline model ability to produce an observed trend: higher-ability models show weaker detection signals under free-$\theta$ estimation at high contamination.
Figure~\ref{fig:theta_scatter} plots baseline accuracy against Cohen's $|d|$ for all model-benchmark combinations.

On MMLU, a negative correlation emerges between baseline accuracy and $|d|$ at 50\% contamination: Mistral (52.4\% accuracy, $|d|{=}3.50$) $>$ Llama (59.3\%, $|d|{=}2.50$) $>$ Qwen (67.8\%, $|d|{=}1.90$).
The explanation is geometric: a model already near the asymptotic ceiling of most item characteristic curves gains less $\hat{\theta}$ from contamination-induced accuracy boosts, but the reduced $\theta$-shift headroom leaves less room for the ability estimate to absorb the aberrance signal.
At 15\% contamination, the pattern is less pronounced because the $\theta$-shift is smaller in absolute terms, leaving a larger proportion of the signal as residual aberrance.

ARC-C reverses this pattern.
Despite Qwen's high baseline accuracy on ARC-C (90.0\%), contamination produces larger, not smaller, effect sizes ($|d|{=}3.16$ at 15\%, $|d|{=}5.30$ at 50\%).
This reversal reflects a ceiling effect: with only 295 items and 90.0\% baseline accuracy, the already-correct items offer minimal room for further $\theta$ inflation, so contamination manifests primarily as anomalous successes on the few remaining hard items.
The small item count amplifies this concentration, producing a disproportionately large $\ell_z^*$ shift per contaminated item.

The baseline $\ell_z^*$ for ARC-C is negative ($-5.42$), in contrast to the positive baselines on MMLU.

These findings indicate that detection sensitivity is not a fixed property of $\ell_z^*$ but depends on the interaction between model ability and benchmark characteristics, a consideration absent from standard person-fit applications.

Llama (59.3\%) shows no benefit from fixed-$\theta$: its high cross-seed $\ell_z^*$ variance ($\text{SD}{=}1.45$ vs.\ Qwen's $0.16$ on ARC-C) inflates the denominator, and its free-$\theta$ estimates are already monotonic ($|d|{=}2.27 \to 2.50$).
The Llama result is itself informative: fixed-$\theta$ estimation is indicated for models with stable clean baselines and high $\theta$-shift absorption (Qwen, Mistral), not as a universal remedy.

\subsection{Preliminary Observation: Post-RL Residual Pattern}
\label{sec:post_rl}

Deployed LLMs undergo reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) or related post-training \citep{ouyang2022, rafailov2023}, which may obscure contamination signals established during SFT.
\citet{wang2025fragility} show that all existing MIA-based detectors fail after post-RL training.
We apply GRPO to a Qwen model contaminated at 15\% on MMLU and track both accuracy and $\ell_z^*$ across training steps.

Figure~\ref{fig:grpo} reveals a dual finding.
First, GRPO erases the accuracy gap between seen and unseen items: the SFT baseline shows 83.1\% accuracy on seen items versus 71.7\% on unseen (a gap of 11.4pp), but after 1,500 GRPO steps, the gap shrinks to 2.1pp (73.2\% vs.\ 71.1\%).
Accuracy-based contamination detection faces a hard boundary at this point.

Second, the $\ell_z^*$ response-pattern structure persists despite the accuracy equalization.
SFT produces $\ell_z^*{=}2.91$; after 1,500 GRPO steps, $\ell_z^*{=}7.69$ (an increase, not a decrease, reflecting model reorganization toward higher overall ability).
The seen-unseen $\ell_z^*$ gap remains at approximately 3.3 ($\ell_{z,\text{seen}}^{*}{=}3.54$ vs.\ $\ell_{z,\text{unseen}}^{*}{=}6.86$), indicating that item-level response patterns retain structural traces of the contamination even after the aggregate accuracy difference disappears.
The $\ell_z^*$ trajectory stabilizes after step 500: all metrics change by less than 3\% between subsequent checkpoints, suggesting a plateau.

This result is $N{=}1$ (Qwen only, 15\% MMLU, GRPO) and carries important caveats: the persistence of the $\ell_z^*$ gap does not constitute proof that contamination is detectable post-RL in deployment, since the gap magnitude and sign may vary with different model families, contamination levels, and RL methods (PPO, DPO).
We report this as a preliminary characterization of the post-RL boundary condition.

GRPO erases the accuracy gap ($11.4\text{pp} \to 2.1\text{pp}$) while the response-pattern gap persists (${\sim}3.3$). $N{=}1$, single model and RL method; no statistical inference is drawn.}
  \label{fig:grpo}
\end{figure}

1	\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}
2	
3	The central question of this work is what binary response patterns can reveal about benchmark contamination.
4	Our findings reveal both the strengths and boundaries of IRT person-fit for this task: $\ell_z^*$ reliably detects SFT-stage contamination across model families, but four boundary conditions constrain its practical utility.
5	
6	\paragraph{Characterization over tool.}
7	The detection-diagnosis tradeoff (\S\ref{sec:degradation}) shows that simpler statistics detect contamination more powerfully than $\ell_z^*$: accuracy $z$-scores yield $|d|$ values several-fold to over an order of magnitude larger, and HT generally exceeds $\ell_z^*$.
8	The value of the IRT framework lies not in detection power but in mechanistic understanding: the $\theta$-shift analysis reveals \emph{why} detection sensitivity varies across models and contamination levels, the seen/unseen decomposition identifies \emph{what fraction} of items are memorized, and the 4PL parameterization captures item-level ceiling effects that 3PL misattributes as aberrance.
9	These diagnostic capabilities are invisible to accuracy $z$-scores or HT.
10	
11	\paragraph{Practical implications.}
12	Two results have immediate consequences.
13	Free-$\theta$ estimation can produce misleading dose-response curves; anchoring $\theta$ to a pre-contamination baseline substantially amplifies detection for high-ability models but is unnecessary where free estimation already captures the signal.
14	The benchmark size boundary means $\ell_z^*$ is most informative for large benchmarks ($n > 7{,}000$ items for 80\% power at 15\% contamination); on small benchmarks like ARC-C (295 items), detection relies on concentrated contamination effects.
15	
16	\paragraph{Scope and calibration.}
17	Universal baseline misfit (57/60 cells flagged) confirms systematic IRT violations; the $\Delta\ell_z^*$ design turns this into a feature through within-model differencing, but requires clean baselines or cross-benchmark references.
18	PSN-IRT provides pre-calibrated 4PL parameters for over 13,000 models \citep{psnirt2026}, enabling retrospective audits of existing benchmark results without additional model access.
19	However, the framework depends on these externally calibrated parameters---information about the item population, not the target model---and our MML-EM refit shows that classical calibration from leaderboard data fails ($r_a{=}0.127$), making the PSN-IRT item bank a critical dependency.
20	ConStat \citep{constat2024} tests distributional shifts requiring multiple benchmarks; $\ell_z^*$ operates on single-benchmark response patterns.
21	The approaches are complementary: ConStat detects performance anomalies across benchmarks, while $\ell_z^*$ provides within-benchmark diagnostic information about item-level response-pattern structure.
22	Parameter perturbation analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:param_perturb}) confirms that $\theta$-fixed detection is robust to ${\pm}10\%$ item parameter noise ($|d| > 3.7$ in all conditions), while free-$\theta$ detection of heavy contamination is sensitive to parameter accuracy---reinforcing the practical recommendation for $\theta$-fixed anchoring (\S\ref{sec:theta_dynamics}).

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

The central question of this work is what binary response patterns can reveal about benchmark contamination.
Our findings reveal both the strengths and boundaries of IRT person-fit for this task: $\ell_z^*$ reliably detects SFT-stage contamination across model families, but four boundary conditions constrain its practical utility.

\paragraph{Characterization over tool.}
The detection-diagnosis tradeoff (\S\ref{sec:degradation}) shows that simpler statistics detect contamination more powerfully than $\ell_z^*$: accuracy $z$-scores yield $|d|$ values several-fold to over an order of magnitude larger, and HT generally exceeds $\ell_z^*$.
The value of the IRT framework lies not in detection power but in mechanistic understanding: the $\theta$-shift analysis reveals \emph{why} detection sensitivity varies across models and contamination levels, the seen/unseen decomposition identifies \emph{what fraction} of items are memorized, and the 4PL parameterization captures item-level ceiling effects that 3PL misattributes as aberrance.
These diagnostic capabilities are invisible to accuracy $z$-scores or HT.

\paragraph{Practical implications.}
Two results have immediate consequences.
Free-$\theta$ estimation can produce misleading dose-response curves; anchoring $\theta$ to a pre-contamination baseline substantially amplifies detection for high-ability models but is unnecessary where free estimation already captures the signal.
The benchmark size boundary means $\ell_z^*$ is most informative for large benchmarks ($n > 7{,}000$ items for 80\% power at 15\% contamination); on small benchmarks like ARC-C (295 items), detection relies on concentrated contamination effects.

\paragraph{Scope and calibration.}
Universal baseline misfit (57/60 cells flagged) confirms systematic IRT violations; the $\Delta\ell_z^*$ design turns this into a feature through within-model differencing, but requires clean baselines or cross-benchmark references.
PSN-IRT provides pre-calibrated 4PL parameters for over 13,000 models \citep{psnirt2026}, enabling retrospective audits of existing benchmark results without additional model access.
However, the framework depends on these externally calibrated parameters---information about the item population, not the target model---and our MML-EM refit shows that classical calibration from leaderboard data fails ($r_a{=}0.127$), making the PSN-IRT item bank a critical dependency.
ConStat \citep{constat2024} tests distributional shifts requiring multiple benchmarks; $\ell_z^*$ operates on single-benchmark response patterns.
The approaches are complementary: ConStat detects performance anomalies across benchmarks, while $\ell_z^*$ provides within-benchmark diagnostic information about item-level response-pattern structure.
Parameter perturbation analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:param_perturb}) confirms that $\theta$-fixed detection is robust to ${\pm}10\%$ item parameter noise ($|d| > 3.7$ in all conditions), while free-$\theta$ detection of heavy contamination is sensitive to parameter accuracy---reinforcing the practical recommendation for $\theta$-fixed anchoring (\S\ref{sec:theta_dynamics}).

1	\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}
2	
3	We presented the first systematic characterization of IRT person-fit behavior for LLM benchmark contamination detection, operating at the minimal-information point of binary response patterns with externally calibrated item parameters.
4	Controlled experiments across three model families ($n{=}10$ seeds each) establish that $\Delta\ell_z^*$ reliably detects SFT-stage contamination (all bootstrap 95\% CIs exclude zero), while revealing four boundary conditions---non-monotonic dose-response, model-specific $\theta$-shift dynamics, a detection-diagnosis tradeoff, and a preliminary post-RL residual pattern ($N{=}1$)---that determine when binary response patterns carry contamination information beyond aggregate accuracy, and when this information is bounded by model ability, benchmark size, and the $\theta$-estimation strategy.
5

1	\section*{Limitations}
2	
3	Our controlled experiments cover three model families (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B) at the 7--8B scale with QLoRA fine-tuning; validation on larger models (13B, 70B), mixture-of-experts architectures, and full-parameter fine-tuning remains future work.
4	The observed negative correlation between baseline ability and detection sensitivity rests on three model families and should be treated as a trend rather than a confirmed relationship.
5	Our findings are scoped to SFT-based contamination and may not generalize to pretraining contamination, which operates through different learning dynamics.
6	The post-RL characterization is $N{=}1$ (Qwen only, GRPO algorithm, 15\% contamination on MMLU); generalization to other model families, RL methods (PPO, DPO), and contamination levels requires further validation.
7	LLMs systematically violate IRT assumptions of local independence and unidimensionality; while the $\Delta\ell_z^*$ design mitigates shared misfit through within-model differencing, the theoretical properties of this correction under severe model misfit remain an open question.
8	The framework depends on pre-calibrated 4PL item parameters from PSN-IRT; parameter estimation errors propagate to $\ell_z^*$ computation, and the approach requires externally maintained parameter banks.
9

The observed negative correlation between baseline ability and detection sensitivity rests on three model families and should be treated as a trend rather than a confirmed relationship.
Our findings are scoped to SFT-based contamination and may not generalize to pretraining contamination, which operates through different learning dynamics.
The post-RL characterization is $N{=}1$ (Qwen only, GRPO algorithm, 15\% contamination on MMLU); generalization to other model families, RL methods (PPO, DPO), and contamination levels requires further validation.
LLMs systematically violate IRT assumptions of local independence and unidimensionality; while the $\Delta\ell_z^*$ design mitigates shared misfit through within-model differencing, the theoretical properties of this correction under severe model misfit remain an open question.
The framework depends on pre-calibrated 4PL item parameters from PSN-IRT; parameter estimation errors propagate to $\ell_z^*$ computation, and the approach requires externally maintained parameter banks.

1	\section{Simulation Validation}
2	\label{app:simulation}
3	
4	Under the null (no contamination), bootstrap $\ell_z^*$ tracks $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$: mean bias 0.041 and standard deviation 1.003 on MMLU.
5	Kolmogorov--Smirnov rejection rates vary with benchmark size: 8.3\% for MMLU and HellaSwag ($n > 10{,}000$), 50.0\% for GSM8K ($n = 1{,}319$), 58.3\% for ARC-C ($n = 295$), and 75.0\% for HumanEval ($n = 164$).
6	$\ell_z^*$ is well-calibrated for benchmarks with $n \geq 10{,}000$ items; smaller benchmarks show increasing finite-sample deviations from normality.
7	
8	Two-sided testing eliminates the inverted-U artifact: MMLU achieves 97.8\% power at 15\% contamination and sustains ${>}$93\% at all levels.
9	Power scales with $\sqrt{n}$, as predicted by the noncentrality parameter $\delta \propto \sqrt{n}$.
10	The empirical power function, derived via Gauss--Hermite quadrature ($K=30$) over the ability distribution, achieves $R^2 = 0.957$ against simulated values, with approximate minimum benchmark size of $n \geq 7{,}958$ items for 80\% power at 15\% contamination under MMLU item parameters.
11	
12	\section{4PL vs.\ 3PL Ablation Details}
13	\label{app:4pl_ablation}
14	
15	Table~\ref{tab:4pl_3pl_power} reports detection power (proportion of 2{,}000 simulation replicates rejecting $H_0$ at $\alpha{=}0.05$, two-sided) for 4PL and 3PL parameterizations across five benchmarks and seven contamination levels.
16	The 4PL model yields higher power than 3PL at every non-trivial contamination level on every benchmark.
17	The advantage is largest on MMLU and HellaSwag, where upper-asymptote ($d < 1$) violations are most prevalent, and smallest on ARC-Challenge and HumanEval, where limited item counts constrain power under both parameterizations.
18	
19	Power is non-monotonic at 75\% contamination under 4PL on four of five benchmarks (e.g., MMLU: $.952 \to .938$; GSM8K: $.846 \to .802$).
20	This reflects the $\theta$-shift boundary condition described in \S\ref{sec:inverted_u}: at high contamination fractions, re-estimated $\hat{\theta}$ absorbs part of the aberrance signal, reducing $|\ell_z^*|$.
21	At 100\% contamination, all items are seen and power reaches 1.000 trivially.
22	The 4PL advantage over 3PL depends on accurate estimation of the upper asymptote $d$; with estimation error exceeding ${\sim}10\%$, the effective model behavior approaches 3PL ($d{=}1$) and the power gain diminishes.
23	PSN-IRT's large calibration sample ($12{+}$ models per item) typically yields $d$ standard errors well below this threshold.

126	\section{Baseline $\ell_z^*$ Interpretation}
127	\label{app:baseline_meaning}
128	
129	The baseline $\ell_z^*$ value reflects a model's difficulty-ordering consistency under the 4PL model, not its accuracy alone.
130	In the empirical data, Mistral ($\text{acc}{=}0.514$, lowest among the 12 models) exhibits $\ell_z^*{=}{+}5.42$ (second highest), because its response pattern follows the IRT-predicted difficulty ordering more closely than higher-accuracy models whose responses violate the assumed item structure.
131	This dissociation explains why Mistral produces the strongest contamination signal despite the lowest accuracy: its lower baseline ability ($\hat{\theta}{=}{-}1.16$) provides greater $\theta$-shift headroom.

162	\subsection{$\Delta\ell_z^*$ Under Local Dependence}
163	\label{app:local_dep}

165	IRT person-fit statistics assume local independence---conditional on $\theta$, item responses are independent.
166	LLM benchmarks violate this assumption through topical clustering (e.g., MMLU subjects); resampling-based approaches can provide valid person-fit assessment even under such violations \citep{sinharay2016}.
167	We evaluate whether the $\Delta\ell_z^*$ differencing design is robust to local dependence (LD) via two simulation scenarios on 14,042 MMLU items with 1,000 replications each.
168	
169	\paragraph{Shared LD.}
